    ⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that for the past several years, most of us made an unspoken deal with inflation.
    • Post midterm elections, inflation is still running hot, but stocks, commodities, crypto are now going the wrong way.
    • If you felt rich in October and feel poor today, you're not alone.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that for the past several years, most of us made an unspoken deal with inflation. Yes, food costs more. Yes, tuition and health insurance went up again. But our stocks, our homes, and our private investments rose even faster. We felt richer, so we shrugged.

    Post midterm elections, inflation is still running hot, but stocks, commodities, crypto are now going the wrong way. Real estate is usually the last domino to fall. We are living in the worst-case scenario for anyone building or preserving wealth: higher prices and lower asset values at the same time.

    If you felt rich in October and feel poor today, you're not alone. My public equity portfolio is overweight tech, and it's taking a beating. I'm down around 20% from the highs, or more than three years of living expenses, and it hurts.

    The only silver lining is that FIRE and debt don't mix, which has prevented me from going on margin and losing even more.

    Say a household has $1 million in investments and spends $120,000 a year. With 3.7% inflation, its cost of living rises by about $4,400 a year.

    Industry observers note that when that portfolio was up 20%, the household gained $200,000. That's 45 years' worth of extra inflation costs. Nobody complains about $4,400 when they're up $200,000.

    Now the portfolio is down 12%. That's a $120,000 loss, and the extra $4,400 a year in living costs hasn't gone anywhere. The household didn't just lose its cushion. It's paying more to live while owning less.

    That's why the mood flipped so fast. The wealth effect works in reverse, and it works faster on the way down. Let's look at how we got here, where stocks could go, and how to survive until the bargain gets restored.

    Recent findings suggest that after Democrats won both the House and the Senate in the midterms, investors began pricing in a slower AI data-center buildout. The market began to correct.

    Recent findings suggest that then Nvidia, due to the Jensen Huang debacle, and the rest of the AI complex kept sliding. The QQQ just finished its 9th-worst week since its 1999 launch, down 10.5%. That's the worst week since March 2020.

    It has been revealed that the S&P 500 closed at 6,910 on Nov 20, about 11.6% below its Oct 6 closing high of 7,819. Another ~9.5% decline to roughly 6,255 and we're officially in a bear market.

    In a recent development, whether you cheered or groaned on election night is irrelevant to your portfolio. The market reprices to future expectations.

    Meanwhile, inflation refuses to cooperate. The last annual CPI reading was 3.7% in September. October prices rose 0.4% month-over-month, hotter than expected. Gasoline is up about 37% from a year ago. And the market is pricing in a Fed rate hike in December.

    Sources indicate that A Fed hiking into a falling stock market is not what the doctor ordered. But it is what we've got.

    Sources indicate that here's what makes this downturn different from 2000 or 2008. Corporate earnings are still projected to grow at a healthy clip. Goldman Sachs forecasts S&P 500 earnings of $375 for 2026, $415 for 2027, and $460 for 2028.

    When stocks fall while earnings rise, the only thing that's breaking is the multiple investors are willing to pay. The S&P 500's forward P/E has collapsed from roughly 23x a year ago to 16.5x today. That's a ~29% de-rating in about 13 months. We're also lower than we were during Liberation Day in April 2025.

    It has been revealed that in other words, the market isn't saying companies are making less money. It's saying it no longer trusts how fast AI profits will grow, and it wants a bigger margin of safety for the risk.

    Here's one of several rosy forecasts by Wall Street firms for year-end 2026 and 2027. I hope it comes true so that my wife and I can keep our FIRE membership card.

    At 6,910 and 16.5x, the implied forward earnings are about $418, which lines up neatly with Goldman's $415 estimate for 2027. So let's run the math using $418 in forward earnings.

    Industry observers note that the first takeaway is counterintuitive. At 16.5x, the S&P 500 is already cheaper than its 5-year and 10-year averages. If valuations simply mean revert to the past decade, the index has 16-20% of upside.

    The bear case states the last decade was the anomaly. Go back to 1990 on the Goldman chart and the aggregate index spent most of the 2003-2015 period between 13x and 17x. Revert to ~15x and the S&P falls another 7-8%. Revert to the 12.8x lows of the post-financial crisis era and we're looking at another ~23% drop.

    Recent findings suggest that but the bigger risk isn't the multiple. It's the earnings. Here's what happens if AI spending gets throttled and forward earnings fall 10% to ~$376, essentially flat versus 2026.

    Sources indicate that the nightmare scenario requires both lower earnings and a lower multiple. That combination gets you to 5,600-5,700, or roughly 28% off the peak. Painful, but in line with a garden-variety bear market, not a 2000-style wipeout.

    My base case is that we're closer to the bottom than the top on valuation, but earnings revisions over the next two quarters will decide whether this is a correction or a bear market. Watch the earnings estimates, not the headlines.

    In a recent development, when stock prices fall, CEOs get nervous and CFOs get busy. The easiest way to defend earnings per share is to cut the biggest expense line: people.

    The layoffs were already happening before the selloff. Through October, tech companies revealed 171,501 job cuts, 21% more than the same period a year earlier, and AI has been the top stated reason for cuts this year. Now add a 10%+ market correction and a Fed that's raising rates. I'm certain more mass layoffs are coming in Q1, after the bonuses are paid.

    I lived through roughly 20 rounds of layoffs during my 13 years at Goldman Sachs and Credit Suisse. The people who got cut first were rarely the least talented. They were the least liked, the least visible, and the most expensive relative to their output.

    Recent findings suggest that so please be on your best behavior if you want to keep your job. Get in first, leave last, volunteer your time, and support your boss's charitable causes. It's corporate theater, but theater keeps the paychecks coming.

    If you don't want to deal with corporate BS anymore, start planning to negotiate a severance package now. The people who get laid off first tend to get the best severance packages. They also get a head start on the hundreds, if not thousands, of employees who will be looking for jobs later.

    Industry observers note that that's what I did in 2012. Instead of quitting, I negotiated my way out with a severance check that helped fund my first years of early retirement. I lay out the whole playbook in How To Engineer Your Layoff. Leaving a job you no longer like with a severance package feels incredible.

    Most downturn advice assumes inflation is falling and the Fed is riding to the rescue with rate cuts. Not this time. When prices go up and asset values go down, you have to defend on four fronts at once.

    It has been revealed that in a bull market, your portfolio can earn more than your salary. In this environment, your paycheck is the only asset that isn't getting marked down every day. Your job is now your most valuable asset, so treat it that way.

    It has been revealed that be the person who uses AI to do the work of two people, not the person AI replaces. Build goodwill with your manager and colleagues before the layoff list gets made. And if you were thinking about quitting, don't. Stick around, collect your paychecks, and see if you can negotiate a severance when cuts inevitably hit your group.

    It has been revealed that if you don't have a second income stream yet, start one now. It doesn't need to replace your salary. It just needs to cover your groceries, which feel like they cost a lot more than they used to. The key to financial freedom is generating enough passive income to cover your basic living expenses.

    If you locked in a low fixed-rate mortgage, congratulations. Inflation is quietly shrinking your debt in real terms. This is not the time to aggressively pay it down and give up liquidity.

    Industry observers note that with the Fed hiking, cash in a money market fund or Treasury bills finally pays you to wait. Earning over 5% risk-free in US Treasury bonds is a beautiful, beautiful thing.

    Sources indicate that favor assets that can reprice with inflation. Rents and replacement costs tend to rise with prices, which is one reason I've always kept a large chunk of my net worth in real estate. Meanwhile, attack the variable expenses that are inflating fastest: gas, food, insurance, and subscriptions you forgot you had.

    Sources indicate that personally, I'm eating less due to rising food costs, which is great for my dad bod challenge. I'm also just fixing my car instead of buying a new one. Finally, I've cut many superfluous items such as cable from our budget.

    Instead of guessing the bottom, tie your purchases to the forward P/E. At ~$418 in forward earnings, 16x is about 6,690 on the S&P 500, 15x is about 6,270, and 14x is about 5,850. If we get down to these levels, buy a slug at each level and let the market come to you.

    Recent findings suggest that before you buy anything, run a Financial SEER check. It's a way to quantify your risk tolerance, calculating potential loss in terms of time.

    Industry observers note that for example, if you have $500,000 in stocks and save $5,000 a month, another 20% drop costs you $100,000, or 20 months of work. If that makes you sick, you're already too aggressive, and buying more won't help you sleep.

    Above all, avoid selling your best assets to fund a lifestyle that inflation made more expensive. That's how a temporary loss becomes a permanent one. Always stay disciplined when there's a chance we're heading into a zombie apocalypse.

    According to recent reports, if you're retired, this is a good time to lower your withdrawal rate and ride it out. As I wrote recently, FIRE in a bear market can actually be comforting. When Return On Effort falls, it's the perfect time to work less, not more.

    If you have kids, a downturn is a gift. use corrections to help make your kids millionaires. During this selloff, I transferred $23,000 into each of my children's custodial accounts and bought stocks. The more the market fell on Friday, November 20, the more I transferred. And I will continue to transfer cash to their accounts and buy if the market goes lower.

    Personally, I've accepted that I can't make money in the stock market right now. Every rally gets sold, and checking my portfolio feels hopeless. So I've stopped trying to fight it. I'm tired of the volatility.

    Instead, I'm spending more time with my kids and fixing things around the house. For a couple of years, thick, heavy wallpaper had been peeling off in our downstairs hallway. It looked terrible, so I finally hired professionals to strip it, patch and sand, then prime and paint the walls. Then I spent an hour filling in imperfections and painting as well.

    It looks great now. When the market won't reward your effort, put your money and energy into something you can actually see improve. This is why having an internal locus of control feels so good. You're not helpless.

    According to recent reports, and please keep living your life. The market doesn't care how miserable you are, so you might as well enjoy the holidays with your family.

    It's easy to forget during a selloff, but downturns are temporary and time in the market is what builds wealth.

    Bear markets transfer wealth from the impatient to the patient. They also reveal who was swimming naked with too much risk, too little cash, and too much confidence in their job security.

    Sources indicate that you don't need to be a hero. You just need to survive with your job, your cash flow, and your sanity intact. Do that, and the next bull market will take care of the rest.

    Readers, are you more worried about losing your job or losing more money in the markets? Where do you think the S&P 500 bottoms if earnings estimates start getting cut? Are you buying the dip in tranches, hoarding cash, or doing nothing at all? And for those who lived through 2000 and 2008 with a significant amount of capital, does this downturn feel different given how strong earnings still are?

    Recent findings suggest that invest In Real Estate To Diversify Away From Volatile Tech Stocks. AI is the next general-purpose technology, but every model needs compute, and compute needs physical data centers, power, and land. That's why I like real estate that benefits from the AI buildout without riding the daily swings of the Nasdaq.     Saddle to Paddle: Bikerafting From Canada to Mexico

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, pete Streufert and his friend Carter (no last name) are cycling 4,025km and packrafting 645km across the U.S.
    • Their route connects the rivers with long-distance cycling trails.
    • Recent findings suggest that before starting the journey on September 17, he said they could find no record of anyone using this particular combination of rivers and cycling routes.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, pete Streufert and his friend Carter (no last name) are cycling 4,025km and packrafting 645km across the U.S. from Canada to Mexico. Starting in Glacier National Park, they will cross four rivers and six U.S. states to finish in El Paso, Texas.

    Their route connects the rivers with long-distance cycling trails. This allows the pair to cross landscapes that would usually require separate trips by bike and watercraft. Streufert, a geospatial wildfire scientist and cartographer, came up with the route by combining existing GPS tracks and geographical data from Bikepacking.com, American Whitewater, and OpenStreetMap. He overlaid cycling corridors and rivers to identify where the two could connect.

    Recent findings suggest that before starting the journey on September 17, he said they could find no record of anyone using this particular combination of rivers and cycling routes. So it is possible that they are the first to do so.

    In a recent development, they started what they neatly call the Saddle to Paddle Traverse on September 17, from Glacier National Park, Montana, on the Canadian border. They kicked off the first packrafting section with a 115km descent of the North Fork of the Flathead River, which forms part of the western boundary of Glacier National Park.

    From there, they followed the Great Divide Mountain Bike Route through Montana toward Jackson Lake, Wyoming, for 1,107km. Here, they hit their second paddling phase on the Snake River.

    It has been revealed that every time they reach a river, the pair inflates their rafts, load their bicycles aboard, and paddle downstream. Then at each takeout, they deflate the rafts, attach them to their bikes, and continue riding.

    It has been revealed that the route. Photo: Pete Streufert.

    Industry observers note that after 130km along the Snake River, their route joined the SLoToJa cycling corridor. They pedaled through Idaho, Wyoming, and Utah. Here, a short connector track took them onto the newly developed Golden Gravel Trail. A further 860km of cycling brought them to Utah’s Green River.

    They then paddled 328km through Desolation and Gray Canyons, including a handful of Class III rapids, and their only Class IV rapid of the trip.

    Sources indicate that pulling their rafts out in Canyonlands National Park, they took the White Rim Trail to Moab. They are now taking a few days in Moab to “get all the mud off our bikes and escape the rain for a day or two before we keep heading south,” notes Streufert.

    From here, they will once again pick up the Golden Gravel Trail through the La Sal Mountains and across Colorado, then continue on the Great Divide Mountain Bike Route to New Mexico.

    Recent findings suggest that paddling the Green River. Photo: Pete Streufert.

    A final paddling section on New Mexico’s Rio Chama will take them to the last leg of the trip, a 950km ride to El Paso.

    It has been revealed that the pair are riding Rodeo Labs Flaanimal 6.0 Steel, fitted with 29-inch Vittoria Mezcal tires, and using Kokopelli packrafts. The pair have described this as a “self-supported” route, although of course they’re replenishing their food along the way. They seem to combine camping with staying in towns.

    View this post on Instagram See this post on Instagram.

    Recent findings suggest that they should complete the journey within the next few weeks, within their two-month timeline. You can follow their progress here.

    Latest Update: Solo Trekker Flouts Khumbu Rules, Evacuated After Cliff Fall

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, A 26-year-old Australian solo trekker who fell from a cliff near Lobuche in the Everest region has been evacuated by helicopter to Kathmandu.
    • Joshua Patrick Cherubino sustained severe head injuries after falling at Kongma La Pass.
    • According to recent reports, kongma La, at about 5,535m, is the highest of the trio of high passes on the classic Everest Three Passes circuit.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, A 26-year-old Australian solo trekker who fell from a cliff near Lobuche in the Everest region has been evacuated by helicopter to Kathmandu. He is recovering in intensive care. By law, all foreign trekkers are supposed to have a guide in the Khumbu.

    Joshua Patrick Cherubino sustained severe head injuries after falling at Kongma La Pass. He was first taken to Lobuche, then flown out on October 27, according to The Tourism Times.

    According to recent reports, kongma La, at about 5,535m, is the highest of the trio of high passes on the classic Everest Three Passes circuit. It links the Chhukung side of the Imja Valley with Lobuche over rocky, non-glaciated moraine. The crossing is long and remote; the descent toward Lobuche is often loose underfoot and comes after hours already spent at altitude.

    Industry observers note that the case has again drawn attention to Nepal’s rules in the Khumbu. Since 2023, the Nepal Tourism Board has required that all foreign trekkers be accompanied by a licensed guide within national parks, including Sagarmatha.

    Sources indicate that in practice, the local Khumbu Pasang Lhamu Rural Municipality has continued to problem its own permits and has not strictly enforced the national guide requirement. Thus, independent trekking remains common on the main Everest routes. Officials quoted by The Tourism Times described unguided travel in the region as a violation of the mandatory rule and a source of preventable rescues.

    Cherubino was traveling alone when he was found. No further details on the circumstances of the fall or his condition have been released beyond the hospital’s assessment that he is recovering.

    Breaking: West Ridge or Hornbein Couloir? Everest Team Prepares for Fourth Attempt

    📅 29 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (632 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • The Russian team is preparing to head up Everest’s West Ridge for a fourth time.
    • Andrei Vasiliev, Vitaly Shipilov, and Sergey Kondrashkin are in Kathmandu recovering from a viral infection and waiting out Cyclone Arnab, which is now weakening.
    • In a recent development, everest West Ridge some days ago.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The Russian team is preparing to head up Everest’s West Ridge for a fourth time. While no easy option exists, they want to avoid the extremely exposed, difficult, and uncertain ridge route. Their only alternative is the Hornbein Couloir, which would force them to stray temporarily into Tibet.

    Andrei Vasiliev, Vitaly Shipilov, and Sergey Kondrashkin are in Kathmandu recovering from a viral infection and waiting out Cyclone Arnab, which is now weakening. They will return to their base in Lobuche this weekend, determined to climb Everest without supplemental oxygen.

    In a recent development, everest West Ridge some days ago. Photo: Andrei Vasiliev.

    Industry observers note that “So far, we have completed three rotations on the mountain,” leader Vasiliev told ExplorersWeb. “Part of this time was spent exploring different options for accessing the route.”.

    Sources indicate that the Russian team has a permit to climb Everest from Nepal, as long as they attempt a route other than the standard Khumbu Icefall-South Col-Southeast Ridge. This has become the normal South Side route since Hillary and Tenzing’s first ascent in 1953.

    Topo of the Russian team’s planned route on Everest, courtesy of Andrei Vasiliev.

    Recent findings suggest that first, the Russians tried to bypass the Khumbu Icefall via the Nuptse Shoulder toward Camp 1, but heavy snow forced them to find another route. Crossing the Icefall (sharing paths with the normal route) was also too hard in the deep snow and on the shaky snow bridges over the innumerable crevasses.

    “Eventually, we selected a third option, via the Lho La,” Vasiliev remarked. “From that pass, our planned route continues across the West Shoulder, along the West Ridge.”.

    In a recent development, at the Lho La col. Photo: Andrei Vasiliev.

    Recent findings suggest that on their latest foray, the team reached 6,400m. “We climbed approximately twelve 60m pitches over rock, snow, and ice of moderate difficulty,” said Vasiliev.

    He noted that on the way to the West Shoulder, they found traces of previous expeditions, including old ropes and snow anchors.

    As for the terrain ahead of them, Vasiliev said:.

    Sources indicate that from our highest point reached, the terrain ahead looks manageable. We can see two more steep rock steps, each approximately 100m high, along with possible bypasses on steep snow slopes. Beyond these obstacles, the terrain appears easier, and we hope to be able to move simultaneously.

    Rocky section on the way to Everest’s West Ridge. Photo: Andrei Vasiliev.

    Vasiliev and his team are confident they can manage this route, despite doing so in increasingly wintry conditions.

    The route linking the Lho La, the West Shoulder, and the West Ridge of Everest has been completed only twice. A Yugoslavian team led by Tone Skarja did the first complete ascent in 1979. They used the Hornbein Couloir variation on their descent.

    It has been revealed that the only repetition was done by a Bulgarian team in 1984. Hristo Prodanov reached the summit on his own and retraced his steps down the ridge but never made it back alive. Some of his partners who summited days later descended via the normal route. Three other teams who climbed the West Shoulder-West Ridge summited by traversing to the North Face, on the Chinese side, and climbing the Hornbein Couloir.

    Recent findings suggest that the North Face of Everest from the West Shoulder. Photo: Andrei Vasiliev.

    Sources indicate that objectively speaking, the Hornbein Couloir offers more summit (and survival) chances than the upper part of the West Ridge. However, it requires traversing into Chinese territory. The Russian team has a permit to climb only from Nepal. It is unclear if a brief border trespass could be considered, and Vasiliev has not confirmed what they will do. “First we need to complete one more rotation,” he noted.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that since 1975, Nikon’s Small World competition has featured images produced by optical microscopes, an art that usually stays in scientific papers and textbooks.
    • Sources indicate that the fruiting bodies of a Hemitrichia slime mold remind one distinctly of Dr.
    • In a recent development, the winning image indicates bubbling globules of black ink being injected onto a piece of paper by an inkjet printer.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that since 1975, Nikon’s Small World competition has featured images produced by optical microscopes, an art that usually stays in scientific papers and textbooks. But through the carefully engineered lenses of the microscope, photomicrographers sometimes capture glimpses of strikingly surreal, alien beauty. The 2026 Photomicrography Competition winners include subjects both living and mechanical, small and very small.

    Sources indicate that the fruiting bodies of a Hemitrichia slime mold remind one distinctly of Dr. Seuss. Photo: Eric Epstein/Nikon Small World.

    In a recent development, the winning image indicates bubbling globules of black ink being injected onto a piece of paper by an inkjet printer. Behind the lens was 25-year-old German design student Ole Bielfeldt, whose work explores the surprising complexity of everyday objects. His process is largely DIY: Bielfeldt builds his own setups, cobbles together parts, and learns techniques online.

    Industry observers note that “I just pick somewhere to start and go for it,” Bielfeldt explained. “You’re likely going to fail at first, and that’s what makes it even more interesting.”.

    The experimentation and imperfection, he added, are the most interesting parts of the process and, ultimately, more vital to him than achieving the highest image quality.

    Photo: Ole Bielfeldt/Nikon Small World.

    In a recent development, ah, mice; the humble martyrs to scientific progress. A significant amount of science seems to involve cutting up mice and learning from the result. But in this sort of photography, even the strongest mouse advocate must admit that the results are visually spectacular.

    Satu Paavonsalo and Dr. Sinem Karaman of the University of Helsinki took this image of a mouse’s eye while researching drug therapy. Photo: Satu Paavonsalo and Dr. Sinem Karaman/Nikon Small World.

    Third place went to another rodent part: a 5X-magnified image of neurons in a mouse’s brain.

    Photo: Kaelin Wulf and Rachel Flannery/Nikon Small World.

    In defense of humanity, we were also willing to subject our own body parts to photographic investigation. The 7th-place winner came from Dr. Bruno Cisterna and Dr. Eric Vitriol at the Medical College of Georgia at Augusta University. Using confocal imaging, which involves scanning a specimen to generate optical sections, they captured human neurons at 20X magnification.

    These human neurons were grown from reprogrammed skin cells. Photo: Dr. Bruno Cisterna and Dr. Eric Vitriol/Nikon Small World.

    In a recent development, I’ll end with a personal favorite of mine, John-Oliver Dum’s image of a little jumping spider, dusted with pollen. Dum, who won second place, credits a childhood bite for his fascination with spiders. The pollen was cultivated by his wife, specifically to create images like this one.

    You can disagree, but I think this little guy is adorable. Photo: John-Oliver Dum.

    You can view the full gallery of winners and honorable mentions here. If you want to see photos of larger things, check out the winners from the Wildlife Photographer of the Year 2026, Aerial Photography, 2026 Ocean Photographer of the Year, or Memorial Maria Luisa International Photo and Video competitions.

    #148231. Tech Report: Thankful Even When Your Wealth And Health Are Both Down

    📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1227 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Financialsamurai ↗ Open Full Page

    Tech Report: Thankful Even When Your Wealth And Health Are Both Down

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1227 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Financialsamurai

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Feeling incredibly sick or losing a ton of money in a very short time.
    • Recent findings suggest that lucky for me, I'm both sick and my public investments are down ~15% from their peak.
    • First, there's feeling dumb for not reducing more risk before the correction.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    I don't know what's worse. Feeling incredibly sick or losing a ton of money in a very short time. What say you?

    Recent findings suggest that lucky for me, I'm both sick and my public investments are down ~15% from their peak. In about 45 days, the market wiped out over three years of our living expenses. Getting beat up both ways hurts.

    First, there's feeling dumb for not reducing more risk before the correction. I've been doing this for over 30 years. I should know better. Greed is a hell of a drug, especially when the 10-year bond yield is at ~5%. And the pain is probably not over.

    According to recent reports, second, there's not being able to function at full strength. Every task takes twice the effort and gets half the result. It's hard for me to breathe and move at the moment. My lungs are bruised from all the dry coughing. Then there's the achy bones.

    If you're thinking about having both spouses retire early, think thrice. When the market tanks and your health falters, having one spouse who still brings in a paycheck and subsidized health insurance is incredibly comforting.

    But I'm still alive and somewhat kicking. So this Thanksgiving, I'm thankful.

    A healthy man wants a thousand things. A sick man wants only one: to feel better.

    When you're sick long enough, your mind starts wandering to dark places.

    What if I don't get better? What if I only get worse? Thank goodness both my wife and I have matching 20-year term life insurance policies to get our kids through to adulthood.

    In a recent development, then my mind wanders to the market. What if this correction turns into a full-blown bear market as Congress throttles AI growth, which may lead to a recession? Anything is possible, which is why having an appropriate net worth allocation by age is important.

    For the longest time, I've kept public equities between 25% and 35% of my net worth. That's the range I'm comfortable with for handling all the funny money volatility.

    But I got lazy and let my exposure drift up to about 45%. Then I got hammered.

    If you're feeling down and out, it's worth going through a list of things you're thankful for. It will make you feel better. Here are some off the top of my head.

    The highlight of the week came on Monday. I felt just strong enough to take the kids and wife to Alcatraz on a gorgeous, sunny San Francisco day, right before the rainstorm rolled in. Tuesday was when my energy began to plummet.

    In a recent development, it was their first time visiting the island, and their first time ever on a boat funny enough. Watching them stand at the railing as the city skyline got larger on our return was a lovely moment.

    There's something fitting about touring a prison while feeling trapped by your own body and a falling market.

    Industry observers note that I spent extra time just sitting in one of the cells, taking in what it would like to be locked up and constantly being told what to do. It brought back old memories when I got in trouble the summer after high school for prank calling. Prison living is the opposite of FIRE living.

    In a recent development, the visit also turned into a real-life lesson for the kids about the consequences of bad decisions. Standing in one of the dark solitary confinement cells will hopefully help them appreciate their nice rooms and the importance of being a good person. That stated, my almost 7-year-old admitted she was a little scared by the end.

    Recent findings suggest that monday reminded me that time with the people you love is the best antidote to a falling portfolio and failing health. It's also the one asset that never comes back once it's gone.

    If you've lost a lot of money and are dealing with a health glitch, or any other personal setback, here's what's helping me. The number one goal is to hang on until the good times return.

    1) Health is the real net worth. No amount of money makes you feel good when you're sick. If you're healthy right now, you're richer than you think, regardless of what your brokerage account says.

    Industry observers note that 2) Measure your losses in time, not dollars. Losing a big chunk of your portfolio sounds catastrophic. But ask how far back the losses take you. Often you're only back to where you were a year or two ago during a correction or bear market. However, if you're sick of work, then a more conservative portfolio adjustment should be made.

    3) Don't make significant decisions while you're sick or distraught. Selling everything at the bottom feels like relief in the moment. It's usually the most expensive relief you'll ever buy. Give yourself a cooling-off period before any major move. Leg out or into positions. No wholesale decisions.

    Industry observers note that 4) Focus on what you can control. You can't control the Fed, AI spending, a CEO's escapades, or a virus. You can control your spending, your asset allocation, your sleep, and how you treat the people around you. Lean into spending time with people and things that bring you the most joy.

    5) Do one thing that gets you outside your head. For me, it was taking the kids to Alcatraz and painting my downstairs hallway. For you, it might be a walk, a phone call with an old friend, or cooking a meal. Action beats rumination.

    Industry observers note that 6) Write down your gratitude list. When your mind keeps spiraling toward worst-case scenarios, putting the good things in writing is a way to fight back.

    Perhaps what I'm most thankful for is the opportunity to try again.

    Industry observers note that we've been through many corrections and bear markets before. None of them ever felt good. But over time, the stock market recovered, and we moved on with our lives.

    According to recent reports, the great thing about being at a low point is that there's likely more upside than downside. Yes, things can always get worse. But unless my illness turns fatal and the stock market falls more than 60%, forcing us to return to work, we'll be OK.

    Sources indicate that finally, I can't talk well enough to record a podcast right now. But I can still move my fingers and write. So I'm thankful for the ability to keep going, no matter what.

    Readers, what are you thankful for this year despite the market correction? Have you ever had to deal with a major financial loss and a health setback at the same time, and how did you get through it? Do you find that losing money makes you more or less grateful for what you have? And what's one thing you proposal to do this holiday season to get out of your own head?

    If you want to build lasting wealth that can withstand corrections like this one, grab a copy of Millionaire Milestones: Simple Steps To Seven Figures, a USA Today bestseller from Portfolio Penguin. And if you're worried about your kids' future in an AI-driven world, keep an eye out for my upcoming book, Your Children Will Be OK.

    College Students Found Dead After Hiking Colorado Mountain

    📅 29 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (506 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that the two young men who set off into Colorado’s Sawatch Mountains this month were both passionate about taking the outdoors seriously.
    • But both of them were found dead Wednesday, under circumstances that remain unclear.
    • The bodies were finally discovered near West Apostle Mountain on October 28, just outside of Gunnison, Colorado.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that the two young men who set off into Colorado’s Sawatch Mountains this month were both passionate about taking the outdoors seriously. One was studying to be a wildland firefighter, while the other hoped to become a mountain guide.

    But both of them were found dead Wednesday, under circumstances that remain unclear. Local authorities spent days looking for missing hikers Kaden Matsuda, 19, and Jackson Donlon, 20.

    The bodies were finally discovered near West Apostle Mountain on October 28, just outside of Gunnison, Colorado.

    Matsuda and Donlon, students at Colorado Mountain College in Leadville, had planned on hiking and camping near Ice Mountain, a 13,960-foot peak located about 50 miles from Gunnison.

    Sources indicate that they left for their trip on Oct. 23. College staff notified local authorities they were missing on Oct. 26, according to the Chaffee County Sheriff’s Office. The men’s families mentioned they were both experienced hikers.

    Matsuda was studying to be a wildland firefighter, and Donlon was training to become a mountain guide.

    Kaden Matsuda, left, and Jackson Donlon. Supplied: Chaffee County Sheriff’s Office.

    Kaden Matsuda, left, and Jackson Donlon. Supplied: Chaffee County Sheriff’s Office.

    Search-and-rescue teams were deployed and found their vehicle at the trailhead. Weather conditions looked risky, with heavy snow falling in Chaffee County.

    Sources indicate that “Ice Mountain is a very technical climb, and it is recommended that hikers be very experienced when trying to tackle it. That is when it is dry. Although there was only about eight inches of snow around Kaden’s vehicle and in the lower basin, Ice Mountain received one to two feet of snow,” the sheriff’s office said in a Facebook post.

    According to recent reports, multiple local SAR teams worked on the case. Photo: Chaffee County Sheriff’s Office.

    Sources indicate that multiple local SAR teams worked on the case. Photo: Chaffee County Sheriff’s Office.

    Rescue teams used drones, helicopters, and dogs to search for the two hikers. On October 27, they located their tent, which had collapsed under the weight of the snow, near West Apostle Mountain (13,597 feet). Inside were sleeping bags, stoves, and other equipment, but the two men were nowhere to be found.

    The next day, authorities declared they had found their bodies in the mountain’s basin. Officials declined to share potential causes of death, beyond stating that they did not suspect foul play.

    It has been revealed that the Sawatch Range of the Rocky Mountains is home to many 13,000- and 14,000-foot peaks. Some of them, like West Apostle Mountain, require technical climbing ability and become substantially more difficult and dangerous during wet weather. The route up the mountain requires traversing fields of loose boulder scree and talus that can be hazardous after snow.

    It has been revealed that from 2010 to 2017, eight people have died in the Sawatch Mountains. Falls are the most common cause of fatalities for those tackling Colorado’s 13ers and 14ers, as the state’s highest mountains are known to locals.

    Latest Update: Rock Spire Collapses at Popular Turkish Tourist Site, Killing Three

    📅 30 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (363 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Explorersweb

    ⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Part of a rock spire known as a fairy chimney collapsed yesterday near the entrance to one of Turkey’s most popular tourist destinations, killing three people and injuring five others.
    • The incident occurred around 3:15 pm local time in the town of Goreme, in central Turkey’s Cappadocia region yesterday.
    • Industry observers note that rescue teams initially recovered two bodies from the rubble before discovering a third victim overnight, bringing the death toll to three.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Part of a rock spire known as a fairy chimney collapsed yesterday near the entrance to one of Turkey’s most popular tourist destinations, killing three people and injuring five others.

    The incident occurred around 3:15 pm local time in the town of Goreme, in central Turkey’s Cappadocia region yesterday. Rocks broke away and fell onto people near the parking area. The site is part of a UNESCO World Heritage landscape, famous for its cave dwellings and cone-shaped rock formations. Nevsehir Governor Huseyin Kok noted that heavy rainfall triggered a landslide that caused the rocks to detach from the formation, according to Reuters.

    Industry observers note that rescue teams initially recovered two bodies from the rubble before discovering a third victim overnight, bringing the death toll to three. The deceased include two Turkish citizens and one foreign national. Five others were injured in the collapse. Some of them were later discharged from hospital, according to AFP.

    In a recent development, eyewitnesses described a loud noise followed by a large dust cloud. The area was closed to the public, and search operations concluded overnight under floodlights.

    Sources indicate that turkish Justice Minister Akin Gurlek said an investigation by the chief prosecutor’s office, along with expert assessments, would begin. The collapse occurred on Turkey’s Republic Day, a public holiday when visitor numbers were high.

    Cappadocia, in central Anatolia, is renowned for its distinctive fairy chimneys. These tall, thin spires of soft volcanic rock topped by harder caps were shaped over millions of years by wind and water erosion. The Goreme Open-Air Museum and surrounding sites were put on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 1985 for their blend of natural landforms and human history, including Byzantine rock-cut churches and underground settlements. The region’s soft rock is geologically fragile and prone to weathering and occasional rockfalls, particularly after heavy rain.

    Turkish authorities have previously carried out restoration and monitoring work to address erosion and climate-related risks, and smaller non-fatal collapses were recorded in the area in 2024 and 2025. The site remains one of Turkey’s most visited destinations, drawing tourists for hot-air balloon rides, hiking, and exploration of its unique geology and heritage.

    Mikel Zabalza, Ruben Perez, and Mikel Saez de Urabain have completed the first ascent of 6,518m Jugal II.

    In a recent development, according to Spanish media, the team climbed via the east-southeast side and reached the summit on October 26. One day later, they returned to base camp, their home team told Diario de Navarra. Zabalza and Urabain had explored the area in the spring of 2024, but bad weather prevented them from attempting the peak. The team will share more details when they’re back home.

    Recent findings suggest that jugal II was also the planned goal for Italians Nives Meroi and Romano Benet, who left for the area three weeks ago. Originally, the team wanted to climb Tilicho Peak in the Annapurna region. Recent storms and floods had cut trails and swept away bridges in that area, so they had to seek an alternative.

    ExplorersWeb caught up with Meroi as she and Benet reached a lodge to seek shelter from the heavy rain.

    In a recent development, “We’re on our way to Kathmandu, and we are with the Spaniards,” she confirmed. As Nives explained, they all attempted the climb, and the Spanish team reached the summit, while the Italians retreated on the previous day. Until now, there has been no news from the Italians since Tine Cuder of Slovenia, the third team member, fell ill and left the expedition two weeks ago.

    Left to right, Nives Meroi, Tine Cuder, and Romano Benet in Kathmandu. Photo: Romano Benet.

    Sources indicate that the Jugal Himal is just northeast of Kathmandu, on the Tibetan border. Surprisingly accessible for a previously unclimbed peak, it’s reachable by bus and a few days’ trekking. Jugal I and II opened to foreign expeditions in 2023. In spring 2024, veteran South Korean climber Um Hong-gil led a Korean-Nepalese expedition featuring Sherpa celebrities Dawa Yangzum and Lakpa Dendi to both unclimbed Jugals. They successfully summited Jugal I, but not Jugal II. According to The Himalayan Database, Jugal II remained unclimbed.

    The main peaks in Jugal Himal. Photo: Nepali News Hub.

    #148226. Piolets d'Or Insider: How the Jury Works, Style Debates, and Future Intends

    📅 30 Oct 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1139 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Explorersweb ↗ Open Full Page

    Piolets d'Or Insider: How the Jury Works, Style Debates, and Future Intends

    📅 30 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1139 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • The recent 2026 edition of the Piolets d’Or awards, held last week in a remote corner of the French Alps, felt like an organization trying to adapt to fast-changing times and attract larger audiences while keeping its prestige and spirit intact.
    • It has been revealed that explorersWeb was there to meet old acquaintances and to put a face to some of the names we wrote about in the last 12 months.
    • Views of Les Ecrins Massif from Saint-Christophe-en-Oisans.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The recent 2026 edition of the Piolets d’Or awards, held last week in a remote corner of the French Alps, felt like an organization trying to adapt to fast-changing times and attract larger audiences while keeping its prestige and spirit intact.

    It has been revealed that explorersWeb was there to meet old acquaintances and to put a face to some of the names we wrote about in the last 12 months. We also wanted to participate in the collective exercise of reflection about the future.

    Views of Les Ecrins Massif from Saint-Christophe-en-Oisans. Photo: Angela Benavides.

    In a recent development, piolet d’Or recipients enjoyed a relaxed atmosphere at the tiny village of Saint-Christophe-en-Oisans and a ceremony at Burg d’Oisans, a 30-minute drive down the valley. Yet, the most interesting event took place the following day, as an elite group of climbers sat around a table in a small hall with large glass windows facing autumn-colored forests and the ragged peaks of the Ecrins Massif, covered in the first snow dust of the season.

    Representing the awardees were Nicolas Jean (awarded for climbing Jannu East with Benjamin Vedrines); the complete teams from Ultar Shar, Aikache Chokk, and Jerupaja Grande; a hyper-energetic, widely smiling Peter Habeler, 84, who received a lifetime achievement Piolet d’Or; Simon Welfringer, who gave a talk; organizers Christian Trommsdorf and David Chambre; geographer and chronicler Rodolphe Popier, and two members of the jury: Jordi Corminas of Spain and Paul Ramsden of the UK. At a press conference, these experts debated some of the hot problems in today’s mountaineering.

    Simon Welfringer of France speaks at the post-Piolets d’Or experts’ panel. Photo: Angela Benavides.

    Recent findings suggest that trommsdorf noted that the jury had an easy time selecting the awarded climbs this year. He explained how these expert jurists choose the best alpine-style activities of the year.

    The members work remotely, choosing from a Big List of outstanding activities. This list is previously compiled by Lindsay Griffin, long-time editor of the American Alpine Journal, and the UK’s Alpine Club. Jurors study the climbs and narrow it down to a short list of candidates, which is not made public. The awards go to those activities chosen by the majority of jury members. In this case, decisions were finalized on the first vote, with no need for a tie-break.

    Sources indicate that left to right, Rodolphe Popier, Jordi Corominas, Paul Ramsden (speaking), and David Chambre. Photo: Piotr Drozdz.

    That led to the first topic of debate: It was noted that some climbing teams happily announce themselves as “Piolet d’Or nominates” on social media when their climbs appear on the Massive List — although organizers make it clear that not all activities on that list are suitable for a Piolet d’Or. Yet, no one supported the idea of making the short lists public. The general agreement was to keep the small “best of the year” finalists available only to the jury.

    The second topic for debate was the presence of a relatively newly introduced piece of technology now ubiquitous on expeditions: drones. These have become essential on rescues, but climbing teams also use them to scout the route ahead. In the near future, drones could also carry supplies, emergency kits, or extra equipment. Commercial outfitters are already using them in this way.

    It has been revealed that benjamin Vedrines and Nicolas Jean of France used drones to check the state of their planned route on Jannu. However, they explained that the drone was useless in relaying information about a section that they couldn’t see from Base Camp. It had a different angle of view, and the drone lost connection when it tried to approach that area.

    Industry observers note that drones piloted by their base camp film crew also hovered overhead as they traversed the long summit ridge. Finally, before the summit push, they used drones to clearly identify the highest point, to make sure they reached the true summit.

    Recent findings suggest that the Ultar Sar team also had a drone, they noted. All the awarded climbers agreed that drones are okay as long as the climbers are completely transparent about what they used them for. Jordi Corominas said the drones are a technological innovation that has come to stay, no different than InReach devices, satphones, or even ice axes and crampons.

    Jordi Corominas, left, discusses past climbs with Benjamin Vedrines. Photo: Piotr Drozdz.

    Sources indicate that interestingly, one jurist stood against the tide: Paul Ramsden is an advocate for the pure alpine-style criteria of the UK climbing school, and with five Piolets d’Or, he is the overall record holder of these prestigious awards. In his opinion, drones spoil the adventure and uncertainty inherent in pure alpine style. Ramsden himself uses neither drones, trackers, nor even satphones.

    Sources indicate that finally, Trommsdor suggested possibly expanding the awards to create a special Piolet d’Or for the best rock climb and perhaps even the best ski descent. The idea expand on the newly introduced performance category introduced this year in the significant list as a test. The category featured, among others, the two Everest ski descents in 2025. Both were heavily supported, and Jim Morrison‘s descent of the Hornbein Couloir was oxygen-assisted.

    In the end, one of the performance ski descents received the female award: Typhaine Duperier‘s alpine-style climb+ski descent of Nanga Parbat’s Schell route, with Boris Langenstein.

    In a recent development, it is unclear whether the latest additions will become official in the near future, but some attendees expressed concern about the context in which these take place. Would they award ski expeditions for their boldness or technical excellence without bearing in mind how the skiers reached the start of their descent (supported climbs, fixed routes, even helicopters)?

    As for rock climbs: where to set the difference between a rock climb and an alpine climb on high, but dry, faces? The debate was left open. We will find out what, if anything, changes in the next edition of the Piolets d’Or.

    Buried houses at the now abandoned village of La Berarde. Photo: Piotr Drozdz.

    The physical award is no longer an actual piolet (ice axe). In the last few years, it has been a hand-crafted trophy that changes with the venue. This time, it was a plaque with a reproduction of Ecrins National Park’s most distinctive peak, La Meige. It rested on a piece of rock from the remains of La Berarde, a nearby village destroyed in a flood two years ago.

    At the Piolets d’Or ceremony in Burg d’Oisans. Photo: Angela Benavides.

    Next year, the Piolets d’Or will be staged in the same location, perhaps in late summer. The event will commemorate the 150th anniversary of the first ascent of La Meige. The long-term plan is to turn the Piolet d’Or ceremony into a bigger, international mountain festival.

    Adventurer to Climb 100 Peaks on 2,000Km Taiwan Traverse

    📅 31 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (663 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that tomorrow, November 1, Japanese adventurer Yoki Tanaka begins a four-month, 2,000km trek north to south down the length of Taiwan.
    • Sources indicate that taiwan has about 268 peaks exceeding 3,000m, but only 100 of them made this special list, which is based not only on height but beauty, difficulty, prominence, and character.
    • Yoki Tanaka arrives in Taiwan earlier this week.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that tomorrow, November 1, Japanese adventurer Yoki Tanaka begins a four-month, 2,000km trek north to south down the length of Taiwan. Along the way, he will summit all 100 of Taiwan’s celebrated Baiyue peaks.

    Sources indicate that taiwan has about 268 peaks exceeding 3,000m, but only 100 of them made this special list, which is based not only on height but beauty, difficulty, prominence, and character. Prominent Taiwanese mountaineers compiled the list in the early 1970s, partly inspired by Japan’s own list of 100 revered mountains.

    Yoki Tanaka arrives in Taiwan earlier this week. Photo: Yoki Tanaka/Instagram.

    In a recent development, the 43-year-old Tanaka has specialized in this unusual combination of long-distance trekking and mountaineering. In 2014, he summited Japan’s 100 famous mountains while walking 7,800km over 208 days. (Japan, though far bigger than Taiwan, has only 23 mountains over 3,000m.) A year later, he extended that by climbing 200 mountains and walking 8,000km in 222 days. Finally, he increased that again to 300 mountains. This time, it took him three years and about 20,000km of walking.

    Tanaka’s projected route across Taiwan.

    Tanaka will begin on Sunday from the northernmost tip of Taiwan, at the Cape Fugui lighthouse, and finish sometime in March at Eluanbi, the country’s southernmost point. The first 150km will be along roads before he reaches his first trailhead. He’ll spend the next week trekking. His first five peaks will be Xueshan (3,886m), Nanhudashan (3,742m), Hehuanshan (3,417m), Qilaishan (3,560m), and Nenggaoshan 3,262m).

    Although he won’t use motorized transport for the entire journey, he will have ample opportunity to resupply along the way. His expedition initiative includes a charmingly precise breakdown of how he looks to spend his evenings: town stays, 48 days; mountain huts, 38 days; tent camping, 39 days. He has also budgeted 16 rest days and 20 contingency days.

    In a recent development, tanaka trains in Taiwan earlier this year. Photo: Yoki Tanaka/Instagram.

    Recent findings suggest that his most difficult section, scheduled for early January, will take him through the remote interior of the Central Mountain Range for over two weeks. During this time, he’ll have to carry his own food, search for trails that may no longer exist, and gamble that he will be able to find enough water.

    During a December 2025 reconnaissance trip to Xueshan, Taiwan’s second-highest mountain, Tanaka discovered how difficult it can be to obtain water. Two water sources marked on his map were completely dry.

    Sources indicate that on a previous hike. Photo: Yoki Tanaka/Instagram.

    According to recent reports, by late January, the Japanese trekker should reach the historic Batongguan Trail, eventually leading to 3,952m Yushan, Taiwan’s highest mountain. The Batongguan Trail was originally constructed in 1875 under the Qing dynasty to establish a route across the mountainous interior. Decades later, Japanese colonial authorities constructed a separate crossing through the region. Sections of the route survive as remote hiking trails and provide access to some of Taiwan’s highest mountains.

    It has been revealed that tanaka first visited Taiwan in the spring of 2025 and has made several reconnaissance visits since, including an east-west crossing of the island earlier this year. He had intended to begin his Taiwan 100 Peaks Traverse project this past spring, but local mountaineers advised him to avoid the rainy season and typhoon risks. Their advice prompted him to shift his starting date to November.

    In a recent development, yoki Tanaka on a training hike in Taiwan. Photo: Yoki Tanaka/Instagram.

    Interestingly, of Taiwan’s 100 Baiyue peaks, only 99 are now recognized as surpassing 3,000m. The exception is Lushan at 2,981m. It was originally measured at 3,043m but subsequent measurements reduced its elevation. Nevertheless, it remains on the list.

    Taiwan’s representative in Japan told Japanese media that the fastest prior completion of the Baiyue by a foreign climber took three years and eight months, spread over multiple trips.

    Once Tanaka begins, his expedition website will provide live tracking of his progress across Taiwan.

    #148223. Breaking: Everest 1971: Ambition, Death, and Dispute

    📅 31 Oct 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1839 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Explorersweb ↗ Open Full Page

    Breaking: Everest 1971: Ambition, Death, and Dispute

    📅 31 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1839 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

    ⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In the spring of 1971, only one party attempted to climb Everest.
    • It has been revealed that it was meant to be as much a test of international cooperation as an extraordinary climbing effort.
    • Recent findings suggest that before the team even arrived in Nepal, the venture was heavily commercialized and advertised to the public.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In the spring of 1971, only one party attempted to climb Everest. Led by Norman Dyhrenfurth and Jimmy Roberts, this ambitious expedition planned to split into two groups. One party would go for the steep Southwest Face, while the other would attempt the West Ridge.

    It has been revealed that it was meant to be as much a test of international cooperation as an extraordinary climbing effort. But what happened turned out to be more complicated and controversial than anyone had expected.

    Recent findings suggest that before the team even arrived in Nepal, the venture was heavily commercialized and advertised to the public. The BBC secured exclusive television rights and embedded a nine-person film crew directly into the expedition. At the same time, the British newspaper rights were sold to The Sunday Times, which sent along prominent journalists like Murray Sayle. The media machinery relentlessly hyped the expedition beforehand, boldly framing the climb as a mere formality and setting public expectations for a historic success.

    Sources indicate that the expedition itself came from a merger of two intends. A British-Norwegian group asked Roberts to lead a Southwest Face attempt. Dyhrenfurth was already organizing the same route, so they joined forces. As the combined team was large, they decided to try two routes at once.

    The Southwest Face was the main goal, specifically aiming for a direct, vertical line (a direttissima), while the other group targeted the complete, aesthetic West Ridge route. Both goals were very difficult, and climbers chose their preferred route.

    Recent findings suggest that jimmy Roberts in Nepal. Photo: The Nepal Times.

    The Southwest Face team included British climbers Dougal Haston and Don Whillans, Japanese climbers Naomi Uemura and Reizo Ito, and others. The West Ridge team included Austrian Wolfgang Axt, Swiss climbers Michel and Yvette Vaucher, Norwegian climbers Odd Eliassen and Jon Teigland, American David Isles, and Indian Major Harsh Vardhan Bahuguna. Frenchman Pierre Mazeaud and Italian Carlo Mauri later joined the West Ridge side.

    In a recent development, in total, the whole expedition had 31 foreign climbers from a dozen countries, as well as several Sherpas, including Ang Phurba and Sonam Girme. According to early planning notes, neither leader had personal summit ambitions. Both described themselves as the older men of the team.

    In a recent development, the Southwest Face of Everest. Photo: Wikimedia.

    Base Camp was established on March 22, 1971, at 5,425m. Both teams worked through the Khumbu Icefall. Dyhrenfurth later said it was in the most difficult and dangerous state he had ever seen it. They set up Advance Base Camp on the Western Cwm, then separated.

    Sources indicate that the Southwest Face team pushed higher. The West Ridge team, with Axt as coordinator, began setting up their own camps, although supplies arrived slowly. Some of the West Ridge climbers didn’t want to carry heavy loads. A long storm in late April made conditions worse for both teams and delayed everything by two to three weeks. Dyhrenfurth’s own account in the American Alpine Journal confirms the early harmony among the team and the exceptional difficulties of the Icefall that spring.

    The 1971 Everest expedition. Photo: ‘Surrender to Everest’/imdb.com.

    On April 18, Bahuguna and Axt of the West Ridge team were descending from a high camp in a storm at about 7,000m. They were not tied to each other. Axt had left his harness and climbing rope higher up to save weight, knowing fixed ropes were already in place. He crossed a long fixed-rope traverse by hand, waited for Bahuguna, saw him wave, then continued down because he was exhausted. He later heard screams and raised the alarm.

    A rescue party reached Bahuguna still clipped to the fixed rope, about 25m from easier ground. He had lost a mitten and a crampon, and his face was covered by ice. Attempts to lower him failed in the storm and darkness, and he finally died of cold and exhaustion. Bahuguna’s fingers and face were crusted with ice, his eyes were wide, and he could not recognize Whillans or speak.

    Major Harsh Vardhan Bahuguna on the West Ridge. Photo: Wolfgang Axt/The Himalayan Journal.

    According to recent reports, according to Roberts’ report in the Himalayan Database, the rescuers had to leave Bahuguna because it would be completely dark in 10 minutes, and the others would freeze too. Roberts later described the death as the result of a series of mistakes by Bahuguna and Axt themselves, and noted that allowing them to go so high alone had been a factor.

    Bahuguna’s body was later recovered and cremated near Base Camp.

    Dyhrenfurth held an inquiry after the fatal incident. Axt noted that the fixed ropes made roping up unnecessary and that he didn’t realize how serious things were until the screams. He later explained that if he had stayed longer, he risked losing his own fingers and toes.

    “What should I do? One hour later and I am frozen,” he noted. He added that he couldn’t pull Bahuguna himself and had to go down for fresh men.

    Mazeaud called it murder through negligence. Dyhrenfurth agreed that Axt should have gone back to look, but noted that it was easy to judge after the event. Roberts noted that Bahuguna’s death was very sad but didn’t determine the expedition’s final outcome.

    Norman Dyhrenfurth, Carlo Mauri, Yvette Vaucher, Reizo Ito, Pierre Mazeaud, and Michale Vaucher in ‘Surrender to Everest’ (1971). Photo: imdb.com.

    After the death and the storm, most of the remaining West Ridge climbers (especially Mazeaud, Mauri and the Vauchers) wanted to abandon both hard routes and switch to the normal South Col route. They said that it was more practical and gave a better chance of reaching the summit.

    Many others, including most of the Southwest Face group and the leading Sherpas, believed that those climbers mainly wanted personal success: first Frenchman, first Italian, or first woman. A vote that included the Sherpas went strongly in favor of putting all remaining effort into the Southwest Face. The West Ridge group stated the decision was a plot to keep them off the summit, so the press would stay focused on the Southwest Face.

    Camp 2. Pumori on the left, with snow-and-ice slopes leading to the West Ridge. Photo: Wolfgang Axt/The Himalayan Journal.

    Sources indicate that mazeaud’s radio message mentioned that they expected him — a French member of parliament — to work like a Sherpa for Anglo-Saxons and Japanese. He said France had been insulted. Yvette Vaucher called the decision monstrous and said she had lost Everest and her friends at the same time.

    According to one account, Roberts told Mazeaud to leave during a loud argument. The four went home in early May, ending further work on the West Ridge. Isles and Teigland later said that the decision to cancel the West Ridge climb, made in a highly emotional moment after Bahuguna’s death, was a great mistake. Teigland said he had dreamed of the West Ridge for two years.

    Industry observers note that A virus, diagnosed by some as mononucleosis, spread through the camps and forced many climbers down, including Dyhrenfurth. Bad weather continued to block supplies. With the West Ridge group gone and fewer people left, Haston and Whillans kept pushing on the Southwest Face. Japanese climbers and Sherpas carried heavy loads high on the mountain. Camps were placed up to approx. 8,290m.

    Haston and Whillans fixed ropes partway into a chimney in the Rock Band but ran out of rope, oxygen, and food. According to Roberts, they placed Camp 6 at 8,290m and were making progress every day. He said they could have traversed onto the South Buttress and reached the summit that way in one day, but that was not the route they had come to climb. Extreme cold hampered them. They needed another camp higher up. They turned back 450m short of the summit on May 21.

    Roberts later noted weather was the basic cause of failure: Once it goes bad, it affects everything else. He described the expedition as 50 percent successful. They failed to summit, but those who stayed worked well together.

    In a recent development, roberts said that he was bitterly disappointed after three years of work, but apart from Bahuguna’s death, he had nothing to regret. He criticized Schloemmer for contributing almost nothing and said that Axt was asked to come up and help on the Southwest Face but thought it over and went down instead.

    Haston called claims that the Austrians were ready to help “complete balls.” He mentioned that when they asked for support at Camp 5, Schloemmer replied that he needed a Sherpa to carry his personal gear. Haston added that he and Whillans were the only ones who could push hard enough to get the route going, and that the Japanese were the only others with real high-Himalayan experience.

    Uemura said that he and Ito helped by carrying loads because that was their obligation, and that if the weather had been good, the expedition could have succeeded. After the 1971 expedition, Uemura decided to always climb solo thereafter.

    Industry observers note that axt and Schloemmer complained there was no real authority above Advance Base Camp. Axt stated the two British stayed high for three weeks and monopolized the lead, and that without a coordinator to rotate people, there was no room for others. He said if there had been good organization on the Face, he could have succeeded. Isles and Teigland said the international aspect had nothing to do with the failure.

    Sources indicate that the problems came from personalities and the emotional decision after the death. Mazeaud and the Vauchers maintained that the leaders had broken the original plan of two routes and prevented them from reaching the summit for publicity reasons. Dyhrenfurth remarked the experiment in international climbing was only partially successful, but cooperation had been good until the argument over the route. He noted that the United Nations had tried international cooperation for a long time and had not done too well, either.

    According to recent reports, in their interesting and detailed post-climb article titled Post-Mortem of an International Expedition for Mountain magazine (later reprinted by The Himalayan Club), authors Ken Wilson and Mike Pearson traced exactly how the initial merger and massive team size doomed the expedition from the start. They concluded that the 1971 expedition’s collapse was primarily driven by severe natural forces, specifically adverse weather and illness, rather than interpersonal friction. They also attributed systemic blame to organizers for combining distinct climbing factions into an unmanageable, oversized team.

    Memorial at Everest in 1971 for Harsh Bahuguna. Photo: Wolfgang Axt/The Himalayan Journal.

    The questions remain: Was Bahuguna’s death mainly the result of mistakes by the two men involved, or something the leaders should have prevented? Did the decision to drop the West Ridge and focus on the Southwest Face save the expedition or destroy it? And was the international idea itself the problem, or simply the mix of strong personalities, bad weather, and the pressure of being on Everest?
